# Key Takeaways from the 2018 AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guidelines

### Key findings

- The 2018 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) feature protocols of stroke care in pre- and in-hospital settings
- Mass General's Thabele Leslie-Mazwi, MD, was one of the authors of the new guidelines
- This article summarizes several of the key takeaways from these new guidelines

The 2018 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) feature protocols of stroke care, including intravenous and intra-arterial therapies, in pre- and in-hospital settings. Thabele Leslie-Mazwi, MD, specialist in Neuroendovascular and Neurocritical Care at Mass General, was one of the authors of the new guidelines. last updated in 2013, which notably expand the window on when thrombectomies can be performed.

### Subscribe to the latest updates from Cardiovascular Advances in Motion

The following are several of the key takeaways for what constitute new recommendations around treatment and overall management of patients presenting with AIS.

01. The primary and secondary goals of patient care are to achieve door-to-needle (DTN) times within 60 and 45 minutes in ≥50% of patients with AIS who are treated with IV alteplase. Neither multimodal CT and MRI (including perfusion imaging) or consideration of endovascular treatment should delay IV alteplase administration.
02. Telestroke/teleradiology evaluations of AIS patients can be as effective for IV alteplase (or acute mechanical thrombectomy transfer) eligibility decision-making as those at stroke centers. Administration of IV alteplase guided by telestroke consultation for patients with AIS can also be as safe. Such decisions should be guided by FDA information on teleradiology systems that support rapid imaging interpretation in time for IV alteplase administration decision-making.
03. Stroke care facilities should ensure brain-imaging studies can be performed within 20 minutes of arrival in the ED in at least 50% of patients who may be candidates for IV alteplase and/or mechanical thrombectomy.
04. Mechanical thrombectomy should be offered to all eligible patients within 6-24 hours of last known normal. Within 6 to 16 hours of last known normal, mechanical thrombectomy is recommended for AIS patients who have large vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation and meet other DAWN or DEFUSE 3 eligibility criteria. Within 16 to 24 hours, mechanical thrombectomy is encouraged should AIS patients meet DAWN eligibility criteria. As part of adherence to either DAWN or DEFUSE 3 criteria or clinical trial protocols, computed tomographic perfusion, DW-MRI, or MRI perfusion can aid in patient selection for mechanical thrombectomy.
05. For patients who otherwise meet criteria for endovascular therapy, a non-invasive intracranial vascular study is recommended during the initial imaging evaluation of the acute stroke patient, although it should not delay IV alteplase. All patients eligible for IV alteplase should receive it.
06. For IV alteplase eligible-patients with mild stroke or those who have previously demonstrated a small number (1–10) of cerebral microbleeds on MRI who are presenting in the 3- to 4.5-hour window, administration of IV alteplase may be reasonable, although treatment risks should be weighed against possible benefits.
07. For patients with minor neurological impairment and no major intracranial occlusion, alternative treatments to alteplase could include tenecteplase administered as a 0.4-mg/kg single IV bolus, which is equivalent but not superior to alteplase.
08. For patients with non-disabling (Modified Rankin (mRS) score 0–2) AIS in the carotid territory who are candidates for carotid endarterectomy or stenting, non-invasive imaging of the cervical vessels should be performed within 24 hours of admission.
09. For patients with minor, non-disabling stroke (mRS score 0–2), between two and seven days of an index event, rather than delay treatment, it is reasonable to perform carotid revascularization for secondary prevention assuming there are no contraindications for this action.
10. In patients presenting with minor stroke, treatment for 21 days with dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel), if started within 24 hours, can be beneficial for early secondary stroke prevention for a period of up to 90 days from symptom onset.
11. Ticagrelor is not recommended over aspirin in the acute treatment of patients with minor stroke.
12. Patients with large territorial supratentorial infarctions are at high-risk for complicating brain edema and increased intracranial pressure and, as such, discussion of care options and possible outcomes should take place quickly with patients and caregivers.

# Mechanical Thrombectomy

The standard of care for acute ischemic stroke with large vessel occlusion continues to evolve.

Media formats available:

[View References](#segment_page_content "View References")

Formats

Choose a format

Mechanical thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) has evolved dramatically over the past decade, during which time results from 6 randomized controlled trials of early thrombectomy1-6 and 2 of later thrombectomy7,8 have established mechanical thrombectomy as the standard of care for patients with AIS harboring a large vessel occlusion (LVO). Meta-analyses9,10 provide invaluable insights into the effect of thrombectomy on patients with LVO strokes. The updated 2018 American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) and European Stroke Organization guidelines have quadrupled the therapeutic time window and support thrombectomy for select LVO strokes up to 16 (Class I) to 24 (Class IIa) hours from time last known well (TLKW).11

Because approximately 30% of patients with AIS have LVO, mechanical thrombectomy has immense potential to prevent severe disability and mortality.12 Every aspect of stroke care from first medical contact to long-term post-stroke recovery is a window of opportunity to increase thrombectomy utilization and improve functional outcomes. It is critical to implement efficient care systems and appropriate triage of patients with AIS using a simplified and permissive patient selection paradigm. This must complement rapid adoption of new devices and techniques for thrombectomy designed to achieve high-quality recanalization with minimum complications. Further understanding of heterogeneity in stroke pathophysiology along with emerging neuroprotective therapies will affect triage, treatment, and ultimately outcomes for those with LVO strokes.

This article provides a review of the updated AHA/ ASA guidelines for management of patients with LVO strokes with an overview of the recently published late-window clinical trials, DAWN[a](http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02142283) and DEFUSE-3[b](http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02586415), and how this information affects patient selection and outcomes. Opportunities to extend the scope of thrombectomy to subgroups yet not studied in clinical trials exist and are the focus of ongoing and upcoming trials. New metrics for technical success of thrombectomy and adjudication of good outcomes are also discussed. Last, the importance of stroke heterogeneity and the existence of distinct stroke phenotypes (fast versus slow progressors) is highlighted (Figure 1).

### Prehospital Triage

Prehospital triage of all patients with AIS to a primary stroke center vs a thrombectomy-capable stroke center depends on various factors: likelihood of LVO, time window of presentation, efficacy of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) for proximal anterior circulation occlusions, and transport time (See [Triage For A Higher Level of Care](http://practicalneurology.com/2019/01/triage-for-higher-level-of-care/) in this issue).

### Patient Selection

Patient selection for mechanical thrombectomy is guided in part by criteria used in recent trials and subsequent recommendations provided by stroke association guidelines.11 Center-specific patient-selection criteria may be broader and depend on conversations between the vascular neurologist, neuro-interventionalist, and the patient and family. Per AHA/ASA guidelines, a patient with AIS who presents within 6 hours may be selected for mechanical thrombectomy with the following demographic criteria: age 18 years or more, NIHSS score 6 or above, and a baseline modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score between 0 to 2. Noncontrast computed tomography (NCCT) and CT angiography (CTA) should be performed to rule out a large territory stroke (< 6) and confirm an anterior circulation LVO (internal carotid or middle cerebral artery [MCA]). Patient selection in the later time window—more than 6 hours—is more complex. Advanced imaging with CT perfusion studies (CTP) or MRI can help delineate an established infarct core and potential mismatch (clinical-core mismatch defined by the DAWN trial, target mismatch defined by the DEFUSE-3 trial).11 Selection in the late-time window may also be simplified—the feasibility of which is supported by retrospective studies.13,14

Eligibility of patients with AIS for thrombectomy in the early and late time window per AHA/ASA criteria is only 11% and 9%, respectively.15,16 The number needed to treat (NNT) in the HERMESc, DAWN, and DEFUSE-3 trials were 5, 2.8, and 3.6, respectively. Limited eligibility (~10%) and large treatment effect (low NNT) suggests that AHA/ASA recommendations are restrictive and some patients who may benefit from thrombectomy may not meet top tier criteria. The decision to treat only the most likely to benefit patients and demonstrate efficacy was an important first step; however, this severely limits the overall benefit of this therapy17 and is at odds with patient preferences.18 It may now be time to consider how to treat the most patients, maximize benefit across all patients with LVO, and reduce overall disability due to stroke. The hesitation of expanding the patient selection criteria is likely due to the perception of increased harm (eg, hemorrhage) in a minority of patients. The authors of this article posit that the outcome would not change in this minority, given the unfavorable natural history of LVO. Limiting therapy would likely expand the number of patients with disability and unfavorable long-term outcome. Broadening the scope of thrombectomy requires extending therapy to types of patients who were not included in clinical trials, including those with a large stroke burden on presentation (ASPECTS score ≤ 5), mild symptoms (NIHSS score ≤ 5), distal occlusions (MCA M2 section and beyond), and strokes with baseline mRS score greater than 2 (Figure 2).

### Procedural Considerations

With increasing thrombectomy utilization and operator experience as well as improving safety profile and thrombectomy devices and technique efficacy, the procedural risk of thrombectomy will continue to diminish. Stent retrievers are recommended for thrombectomy with Class Ia evidence. A meta-analysis including 4 thrombectomy trials where stent retrievers were used confirmed the safety of stent retrievers with comparable rates of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage as well as efficacy with successful recanalization rates (77%).19 Balloon-guided catheters (BGCs) may have higher successful recanalization rates,20 although this has not been demonstrated in a randomized controlled trial setting.

New metrics to adjudicate successful recanalization are being developed. The most widespread scoring system for the degree of recanalization, the modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction Scale (mTICI) has limited interrater reliability and a large magnitude of difference between the degree of recanalization defined by score 2b and 2c/3. A more granular score has been developed and tested, the extended TICI (eTICI) score,21 which can delineate meaningful clinical differences in outcomes based on the degree of recanalization. Another metric for recanalization and an independent predictor of good outcome is the first pass effect (FPE), defined as achievement of complete recanalization (TICI 3) after the first thrombectomy attempt.22 The FPE is associated with the use of BGC and occlusion location does not involve the internal carotid artery (ICA).

Other interprocedural safety metrics are embolization in new territory (ENT), defined as emboli observed on post-thrombectomy angiography within previously unaffected territories, and embolization in distal territory (EDT), defined as emboli seen within the territory of the vessel where the thrombus was originally located both of which can increase procedure time and technical challenges, leading to higher ischemic insult and decreasing likelihood of a good outcome.23,24 Conventional guide-wire—based stent retriever thrombectomy without concurrent aspiration may increase the rates of ENT/EDT. New devices such as EmboTrap II (Cerenovus; with an inner channel inside the stent retriever) may lead to lower rates of ENT/EDT. Using aspiration as first-line thrombectomy technique has been demonstrated to be as good as using a stent retriever.25-27

### Prognosis

Functional independence rates (mRS 0-2) 90 days after AIS due to LVO have increased significantly since the advent of thrombectomy. Thrombectomy outcomes are dependent on age and NIHSS score and ischemic core volume are inversely related to the likelihood of a good outcome.9,28 Prognostication scores like the Pittsburgh Outcomes After Stroke Thrombectomy (POST) Score29 and Houston Intra-Arterial Therapy 2 (HIAT2) score30 have been developed to predict outcome after anterior circulation stroke thrombectomy. Outcomes after thrombectomy are highly dependent on time, particularly in the early-time window. The effect of time exists but is less profound in the late-time window because of patient selection emphasizing those with small ischemic cores and presence of salvageable brain tissue.31,32 Recent data indicate the rate of neuron loss in patients with LVO is highly variable, ranging from less than 35,000 to more than 27 million neurons per minute.33

With respect to outcomes, it is important to consider why only 50% of patients with LVO who have thrombectomy become functionally independent, whether data exists to support thrombectomy in patients with LVO stroke types not studied in clinical trials, and what entails a “good outcome.” The next frontier for mechanical thrombectomy is to further optimize outcomes. Research is ongoing regarding efforts to shorten times to groin puncture, achieve high quality recanalization using new devices and techniques, understand stroke biology for effective triage and treatment (slow versus fast progressors), explore neuroprotective strategies[d](http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02930018), minimize edema[e](http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02864953), and reduce rates of parenchymal and symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.34 Introduction of stem cells in the acute[f](http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03545607) and chronic[g](http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02117635) recovery periods after ischemic stroke are exciting opportunities in the management of patients with AIS who have mechanical thrombectomy.

### Conclusions

Current guidelines regarding thrombectomy for patients with AIS are restrictive. Important types of patients with LVO stroke do not meet AHA/ASA criteria. Data from meta-analysis of 7 thrombectomy trials indicate that mechanical thrombectomy in stroke involving more than one-third of the MCA territory or ASPECTS score of 6 or under provides benefit despite increase in the rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.35 Further analysis of patients who underwent CT perfusion indicates that ischemic core is an independent predictor of functional independence and clinically meaningful treatment effect of thrombectomy exists with increasing ischemic core size.36 Retrospective data regarding thrombectomy in people with mild strokes with LVO is inconclusive.37,38 Equipoise therefore exists and randomized controlled trials are underway including for people with large strokes[h](http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03094715), mild deficits, and mild strokes[i](https://www.inextremis-study.com). Results of these trials may help further expand the indication of mechanical thrombectomy.

The individual’s definition of favorable outcome is important but difficult to elucidate in randomized clinical trials. Functional independence is appropriately used as an efficacy end-point in trials and clinical practice; however, a patient with a large stroke burden or baseline function of mRS 3 may accept mRS 3 or return to baseline as a good outcome. In contrast, in patients with low NIHSS score and distal occlusions, cognition39 or an mRS from 0 to 1 may be a more meaningful measurement of a good outcome.

The field of interventional neurology is expanding rapidly. The incidence and prevalence of LVO stroke and accompanying disability is increasing with a global demographic shift towards the elderly. Mechanical thrombectomy is a powerful tool to treat people with LVO strokes and alter its devastating natural history. Maximizing the potential of this treatment is essential.

# New Stroke Guidelines Extend Thrombectomy to 24 Hours

Pauline Anderson

January 25, 2018

LOS ANGELES — New guidelines for the management of acute stroke include selection criteria for patients to receive mechanical endovascular thrombectomy up to 24 hours after their stroke.

The guidelines are timely because there has been "a sweeping change" in the management of acute stroke since the last guidelines were released, guideline writing committee chair, William J. Powers, MD, H. Houston Merritt Distinguished Professor and Chair, Department of Neurology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told *Medscape Medical News.*

"In 2013, there were no data, no good clinical trial data, that anybody benefited from this procedure, and now there is."

The new guidelines were released here at the International Stroke Conference (ISC) 2018 and [published online](https://stroke.ahajournals.org/content/early/2018/01/23/STR.0000000000000158) January 24 in *Stroke*. The document was endorsed by the American Association of Neurological Surgeons, the Congress of Neurological Surgeons, and the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine.

In 2015, the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) issued a [Focused Update](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/847211) of the 2013 guidelines for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke. Among other things, the evidence-based guidelines covered the selection of eligible patients for endovascular therapy with a stent retriever (mechanical thrombectomy) within 6 hours from the onset of a stroke.

However, since those guidelines were published, two additional studies have suggested that some patients can benefit from the procedure after 6 hours — possibly up to 24 hours following a stroke.

One of these studies — DEFUSE-3 — was presented at this meeting and [published simultaneously](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1713973) in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (*NEJM*) just hours before release the updated guidelines. Guideline authors had the chance to review the manuscript for this trial in advance and include the information in their updated guideline.

"When you talk about up-to-date guidelines, it doesn't get any more up-to-date than this," Dr Powers said.

One of the selection criteria for mechanical thrombectomy is having a large clot in one of the large vessels at the base of the brain. "It's not every stroke; it has to be a large clot," said Dr Powers, that typically cause more severe strokes.

According to the updated guidelines, patients should be considered for thrombectomy in under 6 hours after stroke onset if they meet this criterion and these other criteria:

 Prestroke modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0 to 1;

 Causative occlusion of the internal carotid artery or middle cerebral artery segment 1 (M1);

 Age over 18 years;

 National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score of 6 or greater; and

 Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score of 6 or greater.

What's different from previous recommendations is that patients who are ineligible for intravenous (IV) tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) may now be selected for mechanical thrombectomy within 6 hours.

This new recommendation is a level 1A.

In light of the new results from DEFUSE-3, and a second study called [DAWN](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/888830), published January 4 also in *NEJM*, the new guidelines recommend thrombectomy in eligible patients 6 to 16 hours after a stroke (another level 1A recommendation).

And on the basis of the DAWN results, the procedure is "reasonable" in patients 16 to 24 hours after a stroke (level IIa-B-R).

Dr Powers explained that to garner a level 1A recommendation, two studies are needed. Both DAWN and DEFUSE-3 covered patients for up to 16 hours, but only DAWN covered patients from 16 to 24 hours.

To be eligible for the mechanical clot removal procedure up to 24 hours after a stroke, patients need to meet clear criteria, essentially inclusion criteria for the DAWN trial. "There are certain computed tomography or MRI findings that need to be satisfied," said Dr Powers.

It's not clear how many patients would benefit from the recommendation extending the time frame for mechanical thrombectomy eligibility to 24 hours, he said.

### **Care Plan**

In light of the broadening selection criteria for this procedure, the new guidelines also recommend that hospitals set up a relevant plan of care.

"We know that this procedure can never be available at every hospital in the country," said Dr Powers. "So it's now really, really important for hospitals in the various regions to start coming up with a system of care."

Such a system would include initially sending patients with symptoms to the closest hospital where staff can determine whether they're having a stroke and whether they're a candidate for IV tPA and, if so, administer it.

But hospitals also need to identify potential candidates for mechanical thrombectomy "and to get them to some place that can do it fast," said Dr Powers.

An increasing number of centers across the country can do this, he added. "There are more and more every day."

The Joint Commission, in collaboration with the AHA/ASA, now offers the Thrombectomy-Capable Stroke Center (TSC) certification program. This new level of stroke certification identifies hospitals that meet rigorous standards for performing mechanical endovascular thrombectomy.

This is the fourth level of stroke center certification offered by the Joint Commission and the AHA/ASA; additional certifications include Acute Stroke Ready, Primary Stroke and Comprehensive Stroke.

### **Intense Training**

The mechanical thrombectomy procedure requires highly skilled professionals, be they radiologists, neurologists, or neurosurgeons. It takes at least 2 years of "intense training" to be skilled enough, said Dr Powers.

"Up until a couple of years ago, there wasn't a huge market for people like that, and now there is."

In addition to recommendations regarding mechanical thrombectomy, the new guidelines broaden the eligibility criteria for IV tPA.

"IV alteplase or thrombolysis remains the cornerstone of stroke therapy," Dr Powers said at a media briefing. "Everyone who is eligible for this should get it, and it should not be delayed to determine if they're eligible for another treatment."

Previous guidelines took a "red light/green light" approach for contraindications and indications. But new information emerging since 2013 allowed the guideline authors to increase the number of indications under the "green light" and reduce the number of absolute contraindications under the "red light," said Dr Powers.

Some of what was absolutely contraindicated before is now subject to the judgment of the treating clinician, he said. For example, a dural puncture within 7 days and nonhead major trauma within 14 days "used to be red lights and now this is a judgment call on the part of the treating physician for weighing the risks and benefits of providing the treatment to the individual patient."

Still, sometimes tPA is all that's needed. "If you're eligible for tPA — if it's been under 4 and a half hours since your stroke — you should still get tPA because sometimes it works and dissolves the clot" and you won't need mechanical clot retrieval, said Dr Powers.

Mechanical thrombectomy and tPA "are not mutually exclusive," and patients can receive both interventions, he said.

Patients with severe strokes who meet criteria for tPA should get this treatment, but physicians should not wait to send them for mechanical thrombectomy. "You don't wait; you basically get them as fast as you can to mechanical thrombectomy," said Dr Powers.

At nearby smaller hospitals, staff will often start tPA on stroke patients, put them in a helicopter, and fly them to Dr Powers' center "with the tPA running," he said.

"When they get here, we check to see if they still have a big clot, and if they do, we will take them to mechanical thrombectomy."

Some patients who are not eligible for tPA — for example, those on blood thinners like warfarin — may still be eligible for mechanical thrombectomy, noted Dr Powers.

This could be tremendously useful, he added. "Before this, we would have to tell those people, 'You're anticoagulated and have had a stroke but I can't give you tPA, so I can't do anything.' But now we can."

### **Blood Pressure**

The guidelines also embrace some changes in blood pressure management.

"Primarily, we have now realized that it's okay for the blood pressure to be high immediately after the stroke," said Dr Powers.

If a patient's blood pressure is at least 220/120 mm Hg and he or she didn't receive tPA or endovascular treatment, and there's no other reason to lower the blood pressure, there's no benefit in bringing it down, he said.

"Before, someone would look at a patient with a blood pressure of 200 over 100 and say, 'This is an emergency; we have to give this patient a medication to bring it down.' Now, we know from studies that this doesn't help. It doesn't hurt; but it just doesn't do anything."

Another recommendation is to use intermittent pneumatic compression on all immobile stroke patients to deep venous thrombosis and possible pulmonary embolism.

The compression sleeves that are wrapped around the calf have inflatable balloons that intermittently blow up and down to squeeze the blood out of the veins in the legs.

Before, there was some debate about whether to use these compression sleeves, anticoagulation, or both, said Dr Powers. "We are saying that this works and with blood thinners, we don't know."

And while anticoagulation may reduce pulmonary embolism, there is risk for bleeding elsewhere in the body.

"The overall benefit of blood thinners is not clear; the overall benefit of these compression cuffs is clear," said Dr Powers.

Another revised recommendation relates to carotid revascularization. When revascularization is indicated for secondary prevention in patients with minor, nondisabling stroke (mRS score of 0 to 2), it is "reasonable," the authors write, to perform the procedure between 48 hours and 7 days of the index event rather than delay treatment if there are no contraindications to early revascularization.

"You shouldn't wait. You ought to look to see if they have a blockage within 24 hours and if they do have one, between 48 hours and 7 days you ought to operate on it."  Previous guideline didn't give a time frame, he noted.

In light of cost implications, an important new recommendation is ordering only tests that are beneficial.

### **Pick and Choose**

Some doctors think that the more information they can gather through tests, the better, said Dr Powers. "But the idea of having a routine bunch of tests that you do in everybody is not cost-effective. No test should be routinely performed in everybody with a stroke; you really need to pick and choose which tests you do in which person to answer a very specific question."

Dr Powers provided examples of which tests could be skipped. One is brain MRI. While patients typically get computed tomography in the emergency department to determine whether they have an ischemic as opposed to a hemorrhagic stroke, "The question is, does everyone with an ischemic stroke need an MRI?" said Dr Powers.

The same question could be posed for those who routinely undergo echocardiography, even in the absence of heart disease.

Other routinely offered tests that don't seem to add benefit include those for obstructive sleep apnea and hyperhomocysteinemia and prolonged cardiac monitoring. Clinicians should "stop and think, and order only the ones that matter," said Dr Powers.

This approach will save precious healthcare dollars "but still provide really, really good care, so we aren't compromising quality of care," he said.

The guidelines focus on acute stroke, including the management before arrival at the hospital, in the emergency department, and during hospitalization, but they don't "draw the line" between acute treatment and prevention, said Dr Powers.

"Prevention is part of the acute treatment of patients. Prevention literally starts the day the patient comes in; we look to see if they need to be on a statin; we start them on aspirin or a similar drug; we decide if they need to be anticoagulated — all of that."

Dr Powers stressed that at least half of the guideline committee members were not allowed to have ties to industry, and the ones who did have ties were not permitted to vote and were banned from participating in relevant discussions.

This, he said, represented "a little step further" from previous guidelines, where those with industry ties were just prevented from voting on recommendations.

Asked by *Medscape Medical News* to comment on the new guidelines, Bruce Ovbiagele, MD, professor and chair, Neurology, Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, praised the new document for being "more comprehensive" and more "user friendly" than previous guidelines.

He commended the authors for recognizing that secondary stroke prevention "starts in the hospital," something, he said, that has not been done before.

Dr Ovbiagele noted that the emphasis on not routinely carrying out a battery of tests on all stroke patients is novel and could contribute to cost savings in the system.

*Dr Powers and Dr Ovbiagele have disclosed no relevant financial relationships.*

Multicenter PROBE RCT, 245 patients, 12 centers in Brazil. NCCT/CTA-only selection, 8–24 hours. Functional independence (mRS 0–2): 25.4% vs. 14.3%, adjusted OR 2.56 (95% CI 1.24–5.29, P = 0.012). NNT = 9. [Note: This trial was presented at ISC 2024 and has not yet been published in peer-reviewed form. It was not included in the guideline’s formal evidence review. It is cited here as confirmatory evidence; see Section I.]

#### MR CLEAN-LATE (Olthuis et al., 11 Lancet 2023):

Multicenter RCT demonstrating EVT benefit in the 6–24 hour window using CTA collateral-based selection—a non-perfusion alternative to CTP. Establishes the principle that imaging strategies beyond CTP are effective. [...] AHA guideline methodology integrates multiple lines of evidence—not RCT data alone. The recommendation for NCCT-based EVT selection in the 6–24 hour window is supported by a convergent body of evidence from randomized trials, large multicenter prospective cohorts, multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses, independent expert reviews, and concordant guidelines from other professional societies.

### A. Randomized Controlled Trial Evidence

#### RESILIENT-EXTEND 7 (Nogueira et al., ISC 2024): [...] #### Nogueira et al.16 (Stroke 2021):

Prospective multicenter registry (Trevo Registry and DAWN Trial, 2,008 patients), comparing NCCT±CTA with NCCT±CTA+CTP selection in both early and extended time windows. CTP-based selection was not associated with improved functional outcomes compared with NCCT-based selection in either time window.

### C. Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses

#### Kobeissi et al.4 (Neurology 2023):

Systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 studies, 3,384 patients. Primary outcome: functional independence (mRS 0–2) OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.87–1.22, P = 0.71)—no difference between CTP and NCCT selection. Symptomatic ICH: OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.58–2.04, P = 0.80)—no difference.

# Response to Request for Modification of the 2026 AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guidelines: Endovascular Thrombectomy Imaging Selection in the 6–24 Hour Window

Nestor R. Gonzalez, Shyam Prabhakaran, Kori S. Zachrison, Enrique C. Leira, Mona Bahouth, Joe Broderick

Stroke · 2026-07-31 · 57(9):2939-2948 · DOI: 10.1161/STROKEAHA.126.056726 · PMID: 42535264 · PMCID: PMC13491549

## Keywords

Thrombectomy (MeSH), Stroke (MeSH), Tomography, X-Ray Computed (MeSH — covers NCCT), Perfusion Imaging (MeSH — covers CTP), Practice Guidelines as Topic (MeSH), Patient Selection (MeSH), Time-to-Treatment (MeSH)

## I. Introduction

The writing group acknowledges the correspondence received from the investigators associated with the DEFUSE and DAWN trials, requesting modification of the 2026 AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline recommendations pertaining to imaging selection for endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) in the 6–24 hour window. The correspondence was signed by 20 investigators and requests downgrading of Recommendation 4.7.2 #2 (EVT for anterior circulation LVO, ASPECTS ≥6, NIHSS ≥6, 6–24 hours) from Class 1 / Level of Evidence A to Class 2b / Level C-LD.

After careful review of the correspondence and re-evaluation of the totality of evidence, the writing group respectfully declines the request to modify the published recommendations. This response addresses each concern raised in the correspondence, examines the factual and methodological basis of the arguments presented, and provides the evidentiary basis for the recommendation as published.

Of note, the final print version of the guideline (July 2026) includes corrections and additions to the web-published version that directly strengthen the supportive text and references for Recommendation #2. These corrections—which predate the receipt of this correspondence—add six additional references and a paragraph of supportive text summarizing the comparative evidence between NCCT and CTP selection, including the CLEAR study1 (1,604 patients), STAR registry2 (733 patients), a multicenter study across 66 sites in 10 countries,3 and three systematic reviews and meta-analyses4,5,6. These additions were planned based on the writing group’s ongoing review and are now incorporated in the authoritative print edition.

A note on the evidentiary scope of this response. The guideline’s formal literature review has a defined cutoff date, and certain evidence cited in this response was not available at the time that review was conducted. Specifically, RESILIENT-EXTEND7 had not been published in peer-reviewed form and was therefore not included in the guideline’s evidence base. Similarly, the Zhang et al.8 meta-analysis (J Am Heart Assoc 2025; 12,199 patients across 16 studies) was published after the completion of the literature review. The recommendation as published rests on the peer-reviewed, published RCT evidence (DAWN, DEFUSE-3, MR CLEAN-LATE),9,10,11 the AURORA individual patient data meta-analysis,12 and the large multicenter cohort and meta-analytic evidence that was available at the time of the review 1,2,4,5,6. RESILIENT-EXTEND7 and Zhang et al.8 are referenced in this response as confirmatory evidence consistent with the guideline’s conclusions, not as foundational bases for the recommendation. This distinction is important: the recommendation was well-supported before these data emerged, and has only been further strengthened by them. A response to a post-publication challenge necessarily engages with the evolving literature, whereas a guideline operates from a frozen evidence base.

## II. Clarification of the Recommendation and the Population at Issue

Before addressing the specific arguments, a critical clarification is necessary. The recommendation that the correspondence seeks to modify—Recommendation 4.7.2 #2—applies to patients with ASPECTS ≥6 (small-to-moderate predicted infarct core) presenting 6 to 24 hours from symptom onset. This is not a large-core recommendation. The guideline’s large-core recommendations are separate: Recommendation #3 addresses ASPECTS 3–5, and Recommendation #4 addresses ASPECTS 0–2. The correspondence applies arguments derived from large-core trials (TESLA, SELECT-2, ANGEL-ASPECT) to the ASPECTS 6–10 population, but these are distinct clinical categories addressed by separate recommendations. Recommendation #2 does not rely on large-core evidence.

ASPECTS 6–10 represent the population enrolled in the landmark late-window thrombectomy trials—DAWN, DEFUSE-3, and the majority of patients in MR CLEAN-LATE, RESILIENT-EXTEND, and the other AURORA trials. This is the population with the most abundant randomized trial evidence supporting EVT in the extended window.

## III. Classification of Recommendation and Level of Evidence: Methodological Considerations

The correspondence states that “there are no randomized trial data to support a 1A recommendation for this population.” This claim does not align with how COR and LOE designations are determined under AHA guideline methodology.

As stated in Section 1.5 of the guideline and Table 2 (Applying Class of Recommendation and Level of Evidence to Clinical Strategies, Interventions, Treatments, or Diagnostic Testing in Patient Care): COR indicates the strength of recommendation, encompassing the estimated magnitude and certainty of benefit in proportion to risk. LOE rates the quality of scientific evidence based on the type, quantity, and consistency of data from clinical trials and other sources. COR and LOE are determined independently (any COR may be paired with any LOE).

### A. Level of Evidence A: Definition and Application

Level of Evidence A requires “High-quality evidence from more than 1 RCT,” or “Meta-analyses of high-quality RCTs,” or “One or more RCTs corroborated by high-quality registry studies.”

#### Recommendation #2 defines a patient population:

AIS from anterior circulation proximal LVO, 6–24 hours, NIHSS ≥6, prestroke mRS 0–1, ASPECTS ≥6. The recommendation is to perform EVT in this population to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality. The recommendation is supported by the following randomized trial evidence:

#### DAWN9 (Nogueira et al., N Engl J Med 2018):

RCT, 206 patients, 6–24 hours. Patients had ASPECTS consistent with ≥6 (clinical-core mismatch criteria). mRS 0–2: 49% vs. 13%, adjusted difference 33% (P < 0.001).

#### DEFUSE-310 (Albers et al., N Engl J Med 2018):

RCT, 182 patients, 6–16 hours. Patients had ASPECTS consistent with ≥6 (perfusion mismatch criteria). mRS 0–2: 45% vs. 17%, RR 2.67 (P < 0.001).

#### MR CLEAN-LATE11 (Olthuis et al., Lancet 2023):

RCT, 502 patients, 6–24 hours. CTA collateral-based selection—a non-perfusion strategy. Adjusted cOR 1.67 (95% CI 1.18–2.36). Demonstrated EVT benefit in the extended window without mandatory CTP.

#### RESILIENT-EXTEND7 (Nogueira et al., ISC 2024):

Multicenter PROBE RCT, 245 patients, 8–24 hours. NCCT/CTA-only selection. Functional independence: 25.4% vs. 14.3%, adjusted OR 2.56 (95% CI 1.24–5.29, P = 0.012). Directly demonstrates EVT benefit with NCCT-only selection in the extended window.

#### AURORA Collaboration12 (Jovin et al., Lancet 2022):

Individual patient data meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (DAWN, DEFUSE-3, ESCAPE, REVASCAT, RESILIENT, POSITIVE), 505 patients. Adjusted cOR 2.54 (95% CI 1.83–3.54, P < 0.0001). mRS 0–2: 45.9% vs. 19.3%. No heterogeneity of treatment effect across ASPECTS subgroups.

This evidence base constitutes high-quality evidence from more than 1 RCT and meta-analyses of high-quality RCTs—precisely what LOE A requires. The patients in these trials had ASPECTS ≥6. There is abundant RCT data for this population.

### B. The Conflation of Patient Population With Imaging Workflow

The correspondence’s claim that “there are no randomized trial data” for this population does not distinguish between two categorically different questions:

#### Question 1:

Is there RCT evidence that EVT benefits patients with ASPECTS ≥6, NIHSS ≥6, presenting 6–24 hours from onset? Yes—overwhelmingly, from multiple RCTs and an individual patient data meta-analysis.

#### Question 2:

Is there a dedicated RCT comparing NCCT-only selection versus perfusion-based selection as competing imaging workflows in the same trial? This is a different question entirely—and it is not the question that COR/LOE methodology addresses.

AHA guideline recommendations define clinical actions for patient populations, not for specific imaging workflows. Recommendation #2 states that patients meeting defined clinical and imaging criteria (ASPECTS ≥6, NIHSS ≥6, 6–24h) should undergo EVT. ASPECTS is inherently an NCCT-based (or MRI DWI-based) scoring system—it is not derived from CTP. The recommendation’s use of ASPECTS as the tissue-status criterion therefore already specifies a non-perfusion imaging assessment. The guideline separately addresses the role of additional imaging modalities in Recommendation 3.2 #8 (emergent brain and vascular imaging, COR 1, LOE A) and Recommendation 3.2 #9 (adjunctive CTP/MRI when immediately available, COR 2a, LOE A).

If AHA methodology required a separate RCT for every permutation of a clinical workflow—imaging modality, geographic setting, anesthesia protocol, device type, operator experience—virtually every COR 1 / LOE A recommendation in this guideline and across all AHA guidelines would need to be regraded. This is not the standard, has never been the standard, and would render the guideline system unworkable.

### C. Why the Proposed 2b/C-LD Classification Is Inappropriate

The correspondence proposes downgrading Recommendation #2 to Class 2b / Level C-LD. Under AHA methodology, Level C-LD applies when evidence comes from “randomized or nonrandomized observational or registry studies with limitations of design or execution” or “meta-analyses of such studies.” This does not describe the evidence base for Recommendation #2, which includes multiple high-quality RCTs (DAWN, DEFUSE-3, MR CLEAN-LATE, RESILIENT-EXTEND), an individual patient data meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (AURORA), large multicenter cohort studies (CLEAR: 1,604 patients; STAR: 733 patients), and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses 4,5,6,8. Applying a Level C-LD designation to this evidence base is not consistent with AHA evidence-grading criteria.

## IV. The Guideline Already Incorporates a Strong Recommendation for Advanced Imaging

A key consideration not addressed in the correspondence is that the 2026 guideline already contains a dedicated, high-level recommendation for advanced imaging in the late window. The relevant recommendations, read together, establish a clear and balanced imaging framework:

### Recommendation 3.2 #8 (Class 1, Level of Evidence A):

In patients with suspected AIS and LVO presenting within 24 hours of last known well, emergent brain and vascular imaging (CT/CTA or MRI/MRA) of the cervical and intracranial vessels should be performed as rapidly as possible for EVT selection and treatment planning.

### Recommendation 3.2 #9 (Class 2a, Level of Evidence A):

In patients with suspected AIS and LVO presenting within 6 to 24 hours of last known well, adjunctive CTP, MRI (DWI-FLAIR mismatch), or MR DWI-PWI with automated postprocessing software analysis can be useful in the evaluation for EVT, if immediately available.

The accompanying guideline text further states:

> Advanced tissue imaging with CTP, MR DWI-FLAIR, or MR DWI-PWI was used as an adjunctive tissue selection strategy in most early window, late window, and large-core thrombectomy RCTs. However, because MR CLEAN and THRACE used only NCCT and LVO detection before randomization, adjunctive tissue imaging was not uniformly associated with improved outcomes compared with NCCT/CTA-only evaluation.

The correspondence’s characterization of the guideline as dismissing or undermining advanced imaging is not consistent with the guideline’s explicit endorsement of advanced imaging as useful (Class 2a, Level A) when immediately available—a strong recommendation by AHA methodology standards.

The correspondence requests the addition of a Class 1A recommendation exclusively for mismatch-selected patients while simultaneously downgrading the NCCT-based recommendation to Class 2b, Level C-LD. This proposal would fundamentally alter the clinical framework from one that permits appropriate imaging-based triage (advanced imaging when available, NCCT/CTA when not) to one that effectively mandates CTP as a prerequisite for guideline-concordant care.

## V. Clarification of the RESILIENT-EXTEND Trial Results

The correspondence states that RESILIENT-EXTEND “showed no benefit of EVT over control” and that “benefits for mRS 0–2 outcomes were counterbalanced by evidence of harm.” This characterization does not reflect the trial’s reported findings.

RESILIENT-EXTEND was a multicenter, prospective, randomized, open, blinded-endpoint (PROBE) trial conducted across 12 stroke centers in Brazil. The trial enrolled 245 patients with anterior circulation LVO presenting 8–24 hours from last known well, selected using NCCT and CTA alone (without CTP or MRI perfusion). The key results:

### Functional independence (mRS 0–2) at 90 days:

25.4% (thrombectomy) vs. 14.3% (control), adjusted OR 2.56 (95% CI 1.24–5.29, P = 0.012). This is a statistically significant result.

### Excellent outcome (mRS 0–1) at 90 days:

Also significantly increased in the thrombectomy arm.

### Severe disability or death (mRS 5–6):

OR for mRS 0–4 vs. 5–6 was 0.71 (nonsignificant); OR for mRS 0–5 vs. 6 was 0.58 (nonsignificant).

The primary endpoint (ordinal mRS shift) was not calculable because the proportional odds assumption was violated due to the bidirectional distribution of outcomes. This is a statistical property of the data distribution—it does not negate the statistically significant benefit in functional independence. The trial investigators have explicitly stated that functional independence (mRS 0–2) was the primary measure of treatment efficacy.

The nonsignificant trends toward increased severe disability or death do not “counterbalance” the significant benefit in functional independence. In clinical trials methodology, nonsignificant trends are precisely that—trends that failed to reach the threshold of statistical significance. Using nonsignificant trends to nullify a significant finding inverts standard evidence hierarchies.

### Regarding the age interaction:

the attenuation of benefit observed in patients over 68 years must be interpreted in the context of the population studied. The RESILIENT-EXTEND trial was conducted entirely within the Brazilian public health system, where older patients face cumulative disadvantages—including limited access to rehabilitation, higher comorbidity burden, nutritional deficiencies, and socioeconomic determinants of frailty—that are not generalizable to healthcare systems with more comprehensive post-acute care infrastructure. Notably, a similar age interaction was observed in the original RESILIENT trial13 (early window, same healthcare system), suggesting that this finding reflects population-specific confounders related to frailty and post-procedural care rather than a limitation of the imaging selection strategy. The age interaction cannot be attributed to the use of NCCT-based selection, as it would be expected to manifest regardless of the imaging modality used for patient triage.

## VI. Asymmetric Application of Evidentiary Standards

The correspondence demands RCT-level evidence (Class 1A) for NCCT-based selection while simultaneously citing observational subgroup analyses to support perfusion-based selection. This represents an inconsistent application of evidence standards.

Specifically, the correspondence relies on the Albers et al.14 AURORA subgroup analysis (JAMA Neurol. 2021;78:1064–1071) as evidence that only mismatch-selected patients benefit from late-window EVT. Several methodological concerns merit attention:

### 1. Post-hoc subgroup definition.

The “undetermined mismatch profile” subgroup (n = 132) was defined post hoc within the AURORA pooled dataset. These patients were not prospectively selected using NCCT as an intentional strategy—they came from trials (REVASCAT, ESCAPE, RESILIENT, POSITIVE) that used NCCT/CTA alongside other modalities. The post-hoc identification of these patients as a distinct “undetermined” group introduces selection and classification bias that limits causal inference.

### 2. Statistical underpowering.

With only 132 patients, the undetermined subgroup had limited statistical power to detect a treatment effect. The point estimate (OR 1.59) still favored thrombectomy; nonsignificance (P = 0.17) in a small subgroup reflects inadequate power, not absence of effect. The 95% CI (0.82–3.06) is wide and fully compatible with a clinically meaningful treatment benefit.

### 3. Contradiction with the primary AURORA analysis.

The primary AURORA individual patient data meta-analysis12 (Jovin et al., Lancet 2022) of the same dataset (505 patients across 6 RCTs) explicitly reported: “No heterogeneity of treatment effect was noted across subgroups defined by baseline ASPECTS.” This finding—from the same data—directly contradicts the interpretation that only mismatch-selected patients benefit.

### 4. Uncorrected multiple comparisons.

The interaction test between mismatch subgroups and the undetermined profile (P = 0.03) was not corrected for the multiple subgroup comparisons performed across multiple imaging profiles and time terciles. In the context of exploratory subgroup analysis, an uncorrected P value of 0.03 does not meet accepted thresholds for declaring a definitive treatment-by-subgroup interaction.

By the standards the correspondence applies to NCCT-based selection, the Albers AURORA subgroup analysis would itself merit a classification no higher than Class 2b, Level C-LD. The correspondence authors cannot simultaneously demand rigorous evidentiary standards for NCCT-based selection while relying on evidence that fails to meet those same standards to support perfusion-based selection.

## VII. Addressing the 12–24 Hour Evidentiary Window

The correspondence makes the factual claim that no patients beyond 12 hours from onset were enrolled using ASPECTS-based selection alone in the non-DAWN/DEFUSE-3 AURORA trials. The writing group acknowledges that the four additional AURORA trials (ESCAPE, REVASCAT, RESILIENT, POSITIVE) enrolled patients primarily within their respective time windows, with limited enrollment beyond 12 hours in trials not using volumetric mismatch criteria.

However, several important counter-considerations apply:

First, RESILIENT-EXTEND enrolled patients up to 24 hours using NCCT/CTA-only selection and demonstrated statistically significant benefit (OR 2.56, P = 0.012). This trial directly addresses the evidentiary gap the correspondence identifies.

Second, MR CLEAN-LATE enrolled patients 6–24 hours using CTA collateral-based selection—a non-perfusion imaging strategy—and demonstrated significant benefit (cOR 1.67, 95% CI 1.18–2.36). This establishes that non-perfusion selection strategies are effective across the full 6–24 hour window.

Third, the AURORA primary analysis showed a stronger treatment effect in the 12–24 hour subgroup (OR 5.86) compared with the 6–12 hour subgroup (OR 1.76), with P for interaction = 0.009. Although most 12–24 hour patients were mismatch-selected, this finding demonstrates that the biological window for treatment benefit extends well beyond 12 hours, supporting the recommendation’s time frame.

Fourth, the AURORA authors’ 2022 caveat—“Whether benefit from thrombectomy in the extended time window exists when patients are selected only based on non-contrast CT awaits further clarification from randomized trials” (Jovin et al., Lancet 2022)—was written before the publication of RESILIENT-EXTEND (ISC 2024), MR CLEAN-LATE (Lancet 2023), and three subsequent meta-analyses. The very data the AURORA investigators called for has since materialized and supports the guideline.

Fifth, the combination of ASPECTS ≥6 with NIHSS ≥6 functions as a de facto clinical-imaging mismatch criterion: patients with relatively preserved brain tissue (high ASPECTS) but significant neurological deficit (high NIHSS) inherently demonstrate a disparity between predicted core and clinical presentation that parallels the mismatch concept.

## VIII. Conflation of Screening Exclusions With Treatment Futility

The correspondence argues that because DAWN and DEFUSE-3 excluded patients with ASPECTS 6–10 who lacked a mismatch profile during screening, this constitutes evidence that NCCT-only selection is inadequate. This reasoning contains a fundamental logical error.

Patients screened out during trial enrollment were never randomized and never treated. They provide no outcome data whatsoever. The absence of trial data on these patients does not demonstrate that they would not have benefited from treatment—it demonstrates only that they were not studied within the confines of those particular trial protocols. Exclusion from a trial is a methodological decision, not a clinical outcome.

The writing group does, however, acknowledge that the DAWN and DEFUSE-3 trial populations represent a perfusion-enriched subset of the broader ASPECTS 6–10 population. Patients who met ASPECTS criteria but lacked a mismatch profile were excluded during screening, and therefore the generalizability of those specific trial results to all patients with ASPECTS ≥6 warrants consideration. This is a recognized limitation of inferring population-level treatment effects from trials with additional selection criteria beyond the imaging parameter of interest.

This limitation, however, does not stand in isolation. RESILIENT-EXTEND enrolled patients with ASPECTS-based selection alone (NCCT/CTA without perfusion imaging) across the 8–24 hour window and demonstrated statistically significant benefit for functional independence (OR 2.56, P = 0.012)—providing direct evidence in the broader, non-perfusion-enriched ASPECTS ≥6 population. MR CLEAN-LATE used CTA collateral-based selection—a non-perfusion strategy—and demonstrated significant EVT benefit across the 6–24 hour window (cOR 1.67, 95% CI 1.18–2.36). The AURORA primary analysis reported no heterogeneity of treatment effect across ASPECTS subgroups. And three systematic reviews and meta-analyses comprising over 10,000 patients have demonstrated no significant difference in functional independence between perfusion-selected and NCCT-selected patients. The convergence of these independent lines of evidence—from a trial that enrolled the broader ASPECTS population without perfusion enrichment, a trial using non-perfusion selection, an individual patient data meta-analysis, and multiple observational meta-analyses—addresses the generalizability concern raised by the perfusion-enriched enrollment of DAWN and DEFUSE-3.

## IX. Contextual Considerations for the MR CLEAN-LATE Evidence

The correspondence states that MR CLEAN-LATE demonstrated “a trend toward harm from EVT among patients with the smallest penumbra volumes.” This requires important contextual clarification.

MR CLEAN-LATE11 (Olthuis et al., Lancet 2023) was designed to evaluate collateral-based (CTA) selection—not perfusion-based selection. The trial demonstrated a significant benefit of EVT in the 6–24 hour window using CTA collateral assessment alone, without CTP. This is itself strong evidence that non-perfusion imaging strategies are effective for patient selection.

The penumbra subgroup analysis cited in the correspondence derives from a recently published secondary CTP analysis (Olthuis et al., 15 JAMA Neurol 2025) that examined penumbra as a post-hoc modifier of the treatment effect in a trial that explicitly excluded patients who would have met DAWN/DEFUSE-3 criteria. This post-hoc subgroup analysis of a non-CTP trial has limited ability to define the independent predictive value of CTP-based selection.

## X. The Totality of Evidence Supporting NCCT-Based Selection

AHA guideline methodology integrates multiple lines of evidence—not RCT data alone. The recommendation for NCCT-based EVT selection in the 6–24 hour window is supported by a convergent body of evidence from randomized trials, large multicenter prospective cohorts, multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses, independent expert reviews, and concordant guidelines from other professional societies.

### A. Randomized Controlled Trial Evidence

#### RESILIENT-EXTEND 7 (Nogueira et al., ISC 2024):

Multicenter PROBE RCT, 245 patients, 12 centers in Brazil. NCCT/CTA-only selection, 8–24 hours. Functional independence (mRS 0–2): 25.4% vs. 14.3%, adjusted OR 2.56 (95% CI 1.24–5.29, P = 0.012). NNT = 9. [Note: This trial was presented at ISC 2024 and has not yet been published in peer-reviewed form. It was not included in the guideline’s formal evidence review. It is cited here as confirmatory evidence; see Section I.]

#### MR CLEAN-LATE (Olthuis et al., 11 Lancet 2023):

Multicenter RCT demonstrating EVT benefit in the 6–24 hour window using CTA collateral-based selection—a non-perfusion alternative to CTP. Establishes the principle that imaging strategies beyond CTP are effective.

#### AURORA Collaboration Primary Analysis (Jovin et al., 12 Lancet 2022):

Individual patient data meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (DAWN, DEFUSE-3, ESCAPE, REVASCAT, RESILIENT, POSITIVE), 505 patients. Adjusted cOR 2.54 (95% CI 1.83–3.54, P < 0.0001). mRS 0–2: 45.9% vs. 19.3%. No heterogeneity of treatment effect across subgroups defined by baseline ASPECTS.

### B. Large Multicenter Cohort Studies

#### CLEAR Study (Nguyen et al., 1 JAMA Neurol 2022):

1,604 patients from 15 sites across 5 countries. Compared NCCT vs. CTP vs. MRI selection for late-window EVT. Neither imaging selection modality was associated with reperfusion futility index, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, or mortality differences. Door-to-puncture time was approximately 20 minutes faster with NCCT.

#### STAR Registry (Porto et al., 2 JAMA Netw Open 2022):

733 late-window patients. ASPECTS were comparable between CTP-selected patients (median 8, IQR 7–9) and NCCT-selected patients (median 8, IQR 7–9). Comparable outcomes irrespective of imaging selection modality.

#### Nguyen et al.3 (Neurology 2024):

Multicenter study across 66 sites in 10 countries, directly comparing NCCT-selected EVT vs. medical management in the 6–24 hour window. Provides Class III evidence that NCCT-selected thrombectomy reduces disability and mortality at 90 days compared with medical management alone.

#### Nogueira et al.16 (Stroke 2021):

Prospective multicenter registry (Trevo Registry and DAWN Trial, 2,008 patients), comparing NCCT±CTA with NCCT±CTA+CTP selection in both early and extended time windows. CTP-based selection was not associated with improved functional outcomes compared with NCCT-based selection in either time window.

### C. Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses

#### Kobeissi et al.4 (Neurology 2023):

Systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 studies, 3,384 patients. Primary outcome: functional independence (mRS 0–2) OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.87–1.22, P = 0.71)—no difference between CTP and NCCT selection. Symptomatic ICH: OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.58–2.04, P = 0.80)—no difference.

#### Lin et al.6 (Neuroradiology 2024):

Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 cohort studies, 4,208 patients. Corroborated the Kobeissi findings: no significant difference in functional independence (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88–1.03) or sICH (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.85–1.86) between NCCT/CTA and CTP selection.

#### Dong et al.5 (J Neurointerv Surg 2024):

Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies (3,419 patients). No significant difference in functional independence between the two imaging modalities in either the overall analysis or propensity-matched subgroup.

#### Zhang et al.8 (J Am Heart Assoc 2025):

The most comprehensive meta-analysis to date, 16 studies with 12,199 patients. Functional independence was not significantly different between CTP and NCCT selection (OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.98–1.21). This 12,199-patient dataset—authored by an international consortium—represents the strongest available observational evidence and supports the guideline as published. [Note: This meta-analysis was published after the guideline’s literature review cutoff. It is cited here as confirmatory evidence; see Section I.]

The mortality signal. The writing group takes seriously the consistent mortality signal favoring CTP-selected patients identified across multiple observational meta-analyses 4,5,6, and regards this finding as warranting both transparent acknowledgment and rigorous interpretation. The March 2026 print edition of the guideline addresses the mortality signal explicitly in both the supportive text for Recommendation #2 and the Knowledge Gaps and Future Research section, reflecting the writing group’s commitment to balanced evidence appraisal.

The nature of this signal, however, must be characterized precisely. All contributing data derive from observational, nonrandomized comparisons in which CTP-capable centers differ systematically from NCCT-only centers in ways that plausibly confound the mortality outcome. These include differences in case volume, neurocritical care infrastructure, geographic setting, rehabilitation access, and patient populations—confounders that have not been adequately adjusted in the existing analyses. The CLEAR study further demonstrated that hospitals using NCCT were more likely to perform thrombectomy than CTP-using hospitals, suggesting that institutional selection dynamics differ by imaging capability in ways that affect the comparator populations. It remains uncertain whether the observed mortality difference reflects a true effect of the imaging modality itself or the aggregate influence of these center-level characteristics on post-procedural outcomes.

The available randomized trial data—including RESILIENT-EXTEND and MR CLEAN-LATE—have not reproduced this mortality signal. While randomized trials are not immune to limitations, the absence of the signal in controlled comparisons, where confounding by center-level factors is mitigated by design, warrants consideration when interpreting the observational findings.

The writing group regards the definitive resolution of this question as a priority for future investigation. The NO-SELECT trial (NCT05230914), a randomized noninferiority trial prospectively comparing NCCT with CTP/MRI selection for late-window EVT, is positioned to provide the clarity that observational data alone cannot. Until adequately powered randomized data establish whether imaging modality independently affects mortality, this observational signal—however deserving of continued scrutiny—does not constitute the type of evidence that, under AHA methodology, would justify reclassifying a recommendation supported by multiple high-quality RCTs. The appropriate response to an unresolved question is further research, not premature modification of guideline recommendations that are well-supported by the existing randomized evidence base.

### D. Independent Expert Review and Convergent Guideline Recommendations

The evidentiary conclusions underlying Recommendation #2 are corroborated by independent expert assessments conducted outside the 2026 AHA/ASA guideline process. These reviews were published before the current guideline was finalized, and the concordance between their conclusions and the writing group's recommendations reflects independent evaluation of the same evidence base—not adaptation of one document to another.

#### Nguyen et al.17 (Lancet 2024):

Comprehensive review stating that most patients with NIHSS >5 and anterior circulation occlusion “can be selected with NCCT and CT angiography alone” up to 24 hours.

#### SVIN GAPS Guideline 18(Nguyen TN et al., Stroke Vasc Interv Neurol 2023):

The Society of Vascular and Interventional Neurology independently reviewed the evidence and issued concordant recommendations supporting NCCT-based selection for late-window EVT.

## XI. Response to Proposed Clarifying Statements

### The correspondence proposes adding language stating:

“Current evidence supports the use of penumbral imaging for selection of late-window patients for EVT. When penumbral imaging is unavailable, NCCT with CTA may be used to guide EVT decision-making.”

This proposed language is redundant with existing Recommendation 3.2 #9 (COR 2a, LOE A), which already endorses adjunctive CTP/MRI when immediately available. However, the proposed framing is not neutral: it establishes perfusion as the default and NCCT as a fallback, which is a substantive clinical and policy position not supported by the comparative evidence. The three systematic reviews and meta-analyses cited above demonstrate no significant difference in functional independence between imaging modalities. Framing one as the default and the other as a substitute misrepresents the evidence and would have predictable consequences for treatment access.

## XII. Practical, Economic, and Health Equity Considerations

### A. Global Health Equity

Approximately 80% of the world’s population resides in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where CT perfusion and automated perfusion software are either unavailable or unaffordable. The RESILIENT-EXTEND trial—conducted in the Brazilian public health system—directly demonstrates that EVT benefit can be achieved with NCCT-only selection in resource-limited settings. Downgrading the NCCT recommendation would effectively communicate that patients in these settings should receive a lower standard of evidence-based care.

### B. Time-to-Treatment

The CLEAR study demonstrated that door-to-puncture time was approximately 20 minutes faster with NCCT compared with advanced imaging protocols. In acute ischemic stroke, approximately 1.9 million neurons are lost per minute of delay in reperfusion (Saver JL, 19 Stroke 2006). The time saved by avoiding CTP processing represents a clinically meaningful reduction in tissue loss.

### C. Economic Considerations

Automated CT perfusion software platforms require substantial investment: subscription-based licensing fees, IT infrastructure, ongoing maintenance, and staff training. For community hospitals, rural stroke centers, and healthcare systems in lower-resource settings, these costs can be prohibitive and represent a barrier to EVT access.

### D. The Practical Impossibility of the Proposed Alternative

The correspondence’s proposed modification—adding a Class 1A recommendation exclusively for mismatch-selected patients while downgrading NCCT to Class 2b, Level C-LD—creates an untenable clinical framework. Physicians at centers without advanced imaging would face a liability paradox: treating based on NCCT (now only 2b/C-LD) exposes them to legal risk for deviating from the “standard of care,” while withholding treatment from patients who would benefit according to the totality of evidence is ethically indefensible.

### E. The Ghost Infarct Core Problem

CT perfusion is not infallible. The well-documented “ghost infarct core” phenomenon (Boned et al., 20,21 J Neurointerv Surg 2017; Ospel et al., AJNR 2024) demonstrates that CTP can overestimate ischemic core volume, potentially excluding patients from treatment who actually have salvageable tissue. This systematic overestimation means that some patients classified as “no mismatch” by CTP would in fact benefit from EVT—a limitation not shared by clinical-imaging mismatch criteria using ASPECTS and NIHSS.

## XIII. Conclusion

For the reasons articulated above, the writing group respectfully declines the request to modify the published recommendations. The key points are summarized as follows:

1. The recommendation at issue (4.7.2 #2) applies to patients with ASPECTS ≥6 (small-to-moderate predicted core)—not large-core patients. The correspondence conflates these distinct populations.

2. The claim that “there are no randomized trial data” for this population is incorrect. Multiple high-quality RCTs (DAWN, DEFUSE-3, MR CLEAN-LATE, RESILIENT-EXTEND) and a patient-level meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (AURORA) provide LOE A evidence for this population. The correspondence conflates “no dedicated RCT of NCCT-only selection” with “no RCT data for ASPECTS 6–10 patients.” These are categorically different claims.

3. The proposed COR/LOE reclassification to 2b/C-LD is not consistent with AHA methodology. COR and LOE are assigned based on the totality of evidence for a patient population, not for each permutation of a clinical workflow.

4. The guideline already contains a Class 2a, Level A recommendation (Recommendation 3.2 #9) for adjunctive advanced imaging in the 6–24 hour window when immediately available. The correspondence fails to acknowledge this existing recommendation.

5. The characterization of RESILIENT-EXTEND as showing “no benefit” does not reflect the trial’s reported outcomes. The trial demonstrated statistically significant benefit for functional independence (OR 2.56, P = 0.012) using NCCT-only selection.

6. The primary AURORA individual patient data meta-analysis (Jovin et al., Lancet 2022)12 found no heterogeneity of treatment effect across ASPECTS subgroups, directly supporting the guideline. The secondary subgroup analysis cited by the correspondence (Albers et al., JAMA Neurol 2021)14 examined a smaller subset of 132 patients without prospective mismatch classification; its statistical power to detect a treatment effect in this subgroup was limited, and the interaction test was not corrected for multiple comparisons. These methodological features constrain the inferential weight this analysis can bear in the context of guideline reclassification.

7. The largest meta-analysis available (Zhang et al., JAHA 2025: 12,199 patients across 16 studies)8 demonstrates no significant difference in functional independence between CTP and NCCT selection. Earlier meta-analyses 4,5,6 and a prospective multicenter registry16 are concordant.

8. The writing group acknowledges the consistent observational mortality signal favoring CTP-selected patients identified across multiple meta-analyses. However, this signal derives entirely from nonrandomized comparisons subject to identifiable center-level confounding and has not been reproduced in randomized trial data. The March 2026 print edition addresses this finding transparently, and the writing group regards its definitive resolution as a priority for future research, particularly through the NO-SELECT trial. An unresolved observational question warrants further study, not premature reclassification of a recommendation supported by multiple high-quality RCTs.

9. The proposed modification would create a clinical framework that effectively mandates CTP for guideline-concordant care, with foreseeable consequences including reduced treatment rates, increased treatment delays, and denial of evidence-based therapy to millions of patients in settings without CTP capability.

10. The final print edition of the guideline (March 2026) incorporates additional references and supportive text that further strengthen the evidence base for Recommendation #2.

The writing group remains committed to evidence-based guideline development and welcomes additional data from ongoing and future studies. The NO-SELECT trial (NCT05230914), a randomized trial directly testing the noninferiority of NCCT selection to CTP/MRI in late-window EVT, is anticipated to provide definitive comparative data. Until such data demonstrate inferiority of NCCT-based selection, the guideline’s current framework—which permits both approaches while recommending advanced imaging when available—represents the most evidence-based, equitable, and clinically sound approach.

results.raw_content:
Stroke remains one of the leading causes of death and long-term disability in the United States, with nearly 800,000 people affected each year. Building on rapid advances in stroke care, the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association has published the **2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke**, providing an evidence-based roadmap from symptom onset through acute therapy and early recovery.

### **Why This Update Matters**

The 2026 guideline supersedes earlier iterations by synthesizing a decade of new evidence from landmark clinical trials, registry data, and health systems research. Key goals include:

- **Expanding access to advanced stroke therapies** such as mechanical thrombectomy and optimized clot-busting agents
- **Standardizing imaging protocols** to accelerate diagnosis
- **Introducing the first pediatric stroke guidance** grounded in contemporary evidence

These changes reflect both clinical innovations and a recognition that coordinated systems of care are essential – from prehospital recognition to stroke center workflows – to improve outcomes and reduce disability.

### **Core Guideline Highlights**

**1. Expanded Treatment Eligibility**

The updated recommendations extend criteria for acute interventions, allowing more patients, including some previously considered outside treatment windows, to benefit from advanced therapies like clot removal procedures. Eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) has expanded in selected patients up to 24 hours after symptom onset when advanced imaging demonstrates salvageable brain tissue. Updated guidance also reflects new evidence supporting treatment of certain posterior circulation strokes and selected patients with larger infarct cores based on imaging criteria.

**2. Rapid Recognition and Triage**

Time remains the most critical determinant of outcome in stroke (“time is brain”). The guideline emphasizes rapid, high-quality imaging and protocols that minimize delays, enabling earlier decision-making for reperfusion therapies. Hospitals are encouraged to complete initial brain imaging within 25 minutes of arrival to confirm stroke type and initiate treatment safely. The guideline also reinforces the importance of coordinated regional stroke systems, including direct transport to thrombectomy-capable centers and the use of mobile stroke units to accelerate diagnosis and treatment delivery.

**3. Clot-Busting Medications and Reperfusion Therapy**

The 2026 update affirms the use of intravenous thrombolytic therapy within 4.5 hours of symptom onset for eligible patients. Both alteplase and tenecteplase are endorsed as effective clot-busting medications, with growing evidence supporting tenecteplase as a single-dose alternative that may simplify administration in time-sensitive settings. For certain patients who present beyond the traditional treatment window, advanced imaging may identify those who could still benefit from reperfusion therapy. Patients eligible for both intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy should receive both therapies rapidly and sequentially, without delaying clot removal.

**4. Pediatric Stroke Guidance**

For the first time, specific recommendations address pediatric stroke care, recognizing that although rare, early diagnosis and timely intervention in children can profoundly impact long-term outcomes. The guideline includes imaging recommendations to differentiate stroke from mimics and provides evidence-informed guidance for the use of thrombolytic therapy and, in selected cases, mechanical clot removal in pediatric patients.

### **Implications for Clinicians**

The updates have several practical consequences for providers in both acute and outpatient settings:

- **Prehospital systems:** Emergency medical services should maintain high suspicion for stroke and implement validated recognition tools to expedite transport to appropriate centers.
- **Hospital workflows:** Streamlined imaging, including computed tomography (CT), angiography, and magnetic resonance imaging when necessary, combined with coordinated interdisciplinary stroke teams will shorten door-to-treatment times.
- **Patient selection:** More nuanced eligibility criteria for mechanical thrombectomy and intravenous thrombolysis may increase the number of patients eligible for definitive therapies, especially with refined imaging selection.
- **Follow-up care:** Early rehabilitation and secondary prevention remain essential components of care; clinicians should ensure risk factor optimization after the acute phase.

These recommendations underscore the value of a system-wide approach, not only focusing on individual treatments but also building integrated stroke care pathways that connect EMS providers, neurology teams, and rehabilitation specialists.

### **A Call to Action**

As stroke remains a major public health burden, clinicians across specialties must stay current with evolving guideline recommendations. Integrating these 2026 updates can help reduce disability, improve survival, and ensure more patients receive the right care at the right time.

**Learn more:** Explore CMHC resources on stroke prevention, cardiovascular risk modification, and guideline-based care strategies to further support your practice.

Sources: AHA Newsroom, AHA|ASA Journals
